newsitem.title: USA: Daley to lead U.S. trade mission to Latin America.
newsitem.headline: Daley to lead U.S. trade mission to Latin America.

text.p: Commerce Secretary William Daley said Monday he will lead his first trade mission since taking over the department to Argentina, Chile and Brazil in May.
Daley said the trip reflects the importance of the region to the United States.

"It underscores the administration's commitment to the hemisphere and free trade in the hemisphere and the importance of our potential commercial interest in this region," Daley said in a telephone interview. "It's a fast growing region, estimated to grow by about 5 percent a year between now and the year 2000.
"It's fast growing and some of our competitors are looking at it rather closely, so it is only natural that this is where we should start," Daley said.
The May 11-19 trip will include a stop in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, where the trade ministers from the hemisphere will discuss efforts to create a Free Trade of the Americas Agreement.
The mission is also the first for the secretary since the department developed new guidelines on trade missions in an effort to open them up to more public scrutiny and participation.

The department has just begun the process of selecting business participants, Daley said, adding that he expects about a dozen companies representing energy, telecommunications and other infrastructure sectors to join the mission.
"We know that there are hundreds of potential matters that American business are working on in Latin America right now," he said.
Daley would not say whether the administration will have unveiled long-awaited trade negotiation legislation by the time his trip takes place.

The legislation has been delayed by a dispute between the White House and the Republican-led Congress over labour and the environment. Officials said they have been working behind the scenes to form a consensus that will pass Congress with both Democratic and Republican support.

The so-called fast track legislation would give the administration authority to negotiate trade deals without fear Congress would try to change them. With fast track authority in place, Congress would be able to vote either for or against a trade agreement with no opportunity to amend it.

The legislation is needed for U.S. officials to negotiate an expansion of the North American Free Trade Agreement to include Chile, the first big step in achieving a broader hemispheric free trade agreement by 2005.

The administration has had no fast authority since 1994, and the U.S. business community is anxious for the administration to send proposed legislation to Congress. Willard Workman, who heads the U.S. Chamber of Commerce's international division, said he had hoped the fast track authority would be approved by lawmakers by July.
"Clearly what the government needs to focus on after a hiatus of almost two-and-a-half years is getting an accommodation with the Congress on a trade negotiation authority," Workman said.
He said the United States is losing its leadership role in international trade, particularly in Latin America, while competitors move in to strike deals that disadvantage American companies.
"We've basically conceded the Chilean market to the Europeans," Workman complained. "It's not that Chile is a huge market for U.S. goods, but symbolically it is extraordinarily important."
The European Union has agreed with Chile on a framework for a trade agreement and is looking to strike a deal with Mercosur, which joins Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay in a trading bloc.
